Three routes, one decision you need to make before anything else

530f24621a.a: When buying a resale property in Spain, you need to account for approximately 10 to 12 percent on top of the purchase price. This includes around 7 percent…
530f24621a.e: 115: Fell in Love With the Costa del Sol this Summer & Want to Make the Move? [Start here]
f: That €300,000 property you found on Idealista isn't actually going to cost you €300,000. When buying a resale property in Spain, you need to budget 10 to 12 percent additional costs on top of the purchase price to cover government stamp duty, notary fees, and legal representation. This hidden buffer is essential: cash buyers should plan for 12 percent, while mortgage buyers typically need 10 percent.
How the hidden costs break down

The extra percentage that catches buyers off-guard splits into three distinct expenses. Around 7 percent goes to stamp duty —a government tax on the property transfer—which is the largest single cost. Notary fees account for roughly 1 percent of the purchase price; the notary is a legal requirement in Spain who authenticates the contract and registers the property in your name. Lawyer fees add approximately another 1 percent, covering your legal representation throughout the transaction.

These percentages compound quickly on higher-value properties. On a €300,000 purchase, that 10 to 12 percent translates to €30,000 to €36,000 in additional funds you must have ready before signing. As Warner explains in the episode , this is the number that nobody tells you when you're scrolling through listings—the listed price is never the final cost of your property.
Cash buyers versus mortgage holders

The percentage you need varies depending on your financing structure. Mortgage buyers typically allow for 10 percent extra because lenders usually cap loans at 70 percent of the property value, providing some built-in flexibility. Cash buyers, with no lender requirements and full responsibility for all costs upfront, should set aside the full 12 percent buffer to ensure they're not caught short by miscellaneous expenses or unforeseen charges during the closing process.

3826f965f8.q: Why do properties listed on portals like Idealista sometimes remain active even after being sold?

3826f965f8.e: 116: The Real Cost of Buying Property in Spain Right Now: Here’s What You Actually Need in the Bank
f: In Spain, the real estate market operates without a centralized system forcing agents to remove listings immediately after a sale. Property owners can list their property with multiple agents simultaneously , and when one agent closes a deal, the others may not receive notification, leaving listings active on portals like Idealista long after the property has sold.
Multiple agents, fragmented information

The core issue stems from how the Spanish property market is structured. Unlike some markets with centralized listing databases, agents in Spain operate largely independently, and each agent maintains their own information about a property's status. When you list with Agent A, Agent B, and Agent C simultaneously—a common practice—they may not communicate the moment one of them closes a sale.

This fragmentation creates a lag where the property portal reflects outdated information. The agent who sold the property updates their records, but the other agents may not. If a potential buyer searches Idealista days or weeks after the purchase completes, they still see an active listing because no one has instructed the portal to remove it.
Keeping listings alive to capture leads

Beyond communication delays, some agencies deliberately maintain listings even when a property has been sold or is in a reservation phase. As explained in The Costa Property Podcast , this happens because agencies face supply constraints in the market and use active listings as a lead generation tool.
